---
title: "Joint probability of events"
---

Suppose that we want to know how often a pronoun is both plural and accusative. The word *both* tells us to find an intersection before doing any probability calculation.

Return to the four form sample space

$$
\Omega_4=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
$$

with the probability measure below.

| outcome | probability |
|---|---:|
| *he* | $.20$ |
| *him* | $.30$ |
| *they* | $.10$ |
| *them* | $.40$ |

Let $P$ be the plural event and $A$ the accusative event:

$$
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
$$

and

$$
A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The [**joint probability**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) of $P$ and $A$ is the probability assigned to their intersection:

$$
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A).
$$

We will sometimes abbreviate this quantity as $\mathbb{P}(P,A)$. The comma is shorthand for the intersection. It does not introduce another probability operation.

## Compute the joint probability by hand

Begin with the set operation:

$$
P\cap A=\{\textit{them}\}.
$$

Then apply the probability measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)
&=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}
$$

The result says that $.40$ of the probability mass falls on outcomes that are simultaneously plural and accusative. It does not say that $.40$ of plural forms are accusative. That second statement restricts the comparison to plural forms and will require conditional probability.

## Arrange all joint events in a table

The number distinction $P$ versus $P^c$ and the case distinction $A$ versus $A^c$ divide the sample space into four nonoverlapping intersections.

| | accusative $A$ | nominative $A^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| plural $P$ | *them*: $.40$ | *they*: $.10$ | $.50$ |
| singular $P^c$ | *him*: $.30$ | *he*: $.20$ | $.50$ |
| total | $.70$ | $.30$ | $1$ |

Read one cell at a time. The upper right cell represents

$$
P\cap A^c=\{\textit{they}\},
$$

so its probability is $.10$. The lower left cell represents

$$
P^c\cap A=\{\textit{him}\},
$$

so its probability is $.30$.

The four interior cells are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Their probabilities must sum to one:

$$
.40+.10+.30+.20=1.
$$

The row and column totals are called [**marginal probabilities**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) because they appear at the margins of the joint table. For instance,

$$
\mathbb{P}(P)=.40+.10=.50.
$$

The marginal probability adds across all case values. It answers how much mass belongs to the plural event without requiring one particular case.

## Reconstruct the table in base R

The following code stores the four joint probabilities in a matrix and computes its margins.

```{r}
#| eval: false
joint <- matrix(
  c(.40, .30, .10, .20),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    number = c("plural", "singular"),
    case = c("accusative", "nominative")
  )
)

joint
rowSums(joint)
colSums(joint)
sum(joint)
```

The row sums are $.50$ and $.50$, the column sums are $.70$ and $.30$, and the full sum is one. These checks expose a transposed or omitted cell before it affects later calculations.

## Interpret the joint object

A joint probability preserves two distinctions at once. This makes the table more informative than either margin alone. Two corpora can both have $\mathbb{P}(P)=.50$ and $\mathbb{P}(A)=.70$ while placing different amounts of mass in $P\cap A$.

For a linguistic analysis, the joint table is often the first place to inspect whether a proposed association is even present. If plural forms are much more often accusative than singular forms, the relevant difference must appear in how mass is arranged across the four cells, not merely in the two margins.

## Using a marginal probability for an intersection

A marginal probability cannot replace an intersection probability. In the toy model, $\mathbb{P}(A)=.70$ includes both *him* and *them*. It cannot answer the question about forms that are both plural and accusative because it also includes singular accusative mass.

The repair is grammatical as much as mathematical. Translate *and* into an intersection, list the outcomes in that intersection, and only then apply $\mathbb{P}$.

## Check your understanding

1. Write the event represented by each of the four interior cells in the table.
2. Compute $\mathbb{P}(P^c\cap A^c)$ by listing the outcomes first.
3. Explain why $\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40$ does not mean that $40\%$ of plural forms are accusative.
4. Construct a different four cell table with the same row and column margins but with $\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.35$.

Joint probability measures the overlap in the full sample space. The [next page](conditional-probability.qmd) restricts the relevant space to one event and rescales the mass within it.
